findings.title: Rebalance Swaps Have Zero Slippage Protection Enabling Sandwich Attacks
findings.description: Both _executeBuy() and _executeSell() pass 0 as the minimum return amount when calling the OKX DEX router's uniswapV3SwapTo(). Combined with rebalance() being publicly callable, this creates a perfect sandwich attack opportunity on Ethereum mainnet. MEV bots can front-run rebalance transactions by manipulating V3 pool price, then back-run to extract profit. PoC demonstrates 54% profit reduction and +1.553 ETH attacker gain from 5 ETH rebalance.

findings.title: createLaunchPadAndInitialBuy() Hardcodes minReturn=0
findings.description: The createLaunchPadAndInitialBuy() function hardcodes minReturn = 0 when calling _buyQuote(), giving callers no slippage protection on their initial buy. The function interface does not accept a minReturn parameter. Although the practical risk for the very first buy is limited because reserves are predictable from virtual liquidity, the design pattern of hardcoding zero slippage is a security anti-pattern.

findings.title: cashIn() Mints msg.value Instead of amount Parameter
findings.description: cashIn() always mints msg.value worth of vTokens regardless of the amount parameter. For the current vETH deployment with NATIVE_TOKEN, require(msg.value == amount) masks this bug. For any ERC20 underlying deployment, the function is completely broken: an attacker can call cashIn(0) with msg.value = 0, transfer no ERC20 tokens, and receive 0 vTokens—or more critically, in a hypothetical misconfiguration mint unbacked vTokens.

findings.title: _buyQuote() Sends Fee Before Reading Reserves (CEI Violation)
findings.description: Fee is sent to owner() via .call{value: fee} BEFORE reading Uniswap V2 reserves. If owner is a contract, its receive() callback executes with the ability to interact with VirtualToken or the pool, potentially manipulating reserves before the router reads them. This violates the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern.

findings.title: Owner Can Set Fee Rate to 100%
findings.description: updateFeeRate() allows the owner to set feeRate up to feeDenominator (10000), meaning a 100% fee. All buy/sell operations would have their entire value taken as fee. While the owner is trusted per README, this represents a significant centralization and rug-pull risk with no upper cap on fees.

findings.title: No Minimum virtualLiquidityAmount in createLaunchPad()
findings.description: The virtualLiquidityAmount parameter has no minimum check. Creating pools with extremely small virtual liquidity (e.g., 1 wei) results in pools with extreme price sensitivity where tiny swaps cause massive price swings, enabling price manipulation attacks.

findings.title: repayLoan() Burns Tokens From Any Address Without Approval
findings.description: repayLoan() calls _burn(to, amount) which bypasses allowance checks. A valid factory can unilaterally burn tokens from any indebted address and reduce their debt, manipulating pool reserves. While factories are trusted, this function is currently unused and represents unnecessary attack surface.

findings.title: rebalance() Is Permissionless
findings.description: Anyone can call rebalance() with arbitrary parameters. Combined with zero slippage protection in _executeBuy/_executeSell, attackers can manipulate V3 pool price, trigger rebalance, and extract value via sandwich attacks. No access control exists on the function.

findings.title: createLaunchPad() Is Permissionless - Enables Loan Limit DoS
findings.description: The onlyWhiteListed(virtualLiquidityToken) modifier only checks that vETH is whitelisted, NOT that the caller is authorized. Anyone can create launchpads, consuming the 300 ETH per-block loan limit and blocking legitimate users. Also enables token name squatting.

findings.title: Protocol DoS If Owner Contract Cannot Receive ETH
findings.description: Both _buyQuote() and _sellQuote() send fees to owner() via call{value: fee} with a require(success). If the owner is a multisig that temporarily cannot receive ETH (paused, upgraded), ALL trading halts. This is a systemic availability risk that can be triggered by owner configuration changes.

findings.title: _buyQuote() Refund Off-By-One Error
findings.description: The refund calculation msg.value - amountXIn - fee - 1 silently keeps 1 wei per buy transaction. Over millions of transactions, the router accumulates irrecoverable ETH dust. The router also has no extraction function to recover this dust.

findings.title: UUPS Implementation Missing _disableInitializers()
findings.description: The UUPS upgradeable implementation contract lacks _disableInitializers() in its constructor. An attacker could initialize the implementation directly and call upgradeToAndCall() to point it to malicious code. Impact is limited since users interact with the proxy, not the implementation.

findings.title: LamboToken Implementation Can Be Initialized By Anyone
findings.description: The implementation contract's initialize() has no access control beyond _totalSupply == 0. Anyone can initialize it, minting tokens to themselves. Impact is minimal since ownership transfers to address(0) and the minted tokens have no utility on the implementation contract.

findings.title: _sellQuote() ETH Transfer Ordering
findings.description: ETH is sent to user BEFORE fee is sent to owner. The user's receive() callback executes before fee transfer completes. Impact is limited by the nonReentrant guard, but this still violates the CEI pattern.

findings.title: amountOut Parameter in rebalance() Is Unused Dead Code
findings.description: The amountOut parameter is decoded in onMorphoFlashLoan() but never used in any logic, indicating incomplete slippage protection implementation. The dead parameter suggests slippage protection was planned but not implemented.

findings.title: takeLoan() Has Unnecessary payable Modifier
findings.description: The payable modifier on takeLoan() serves no purpose—the function logic does not use msg.value. Any ETH sent with takeLoan is permanently locked in the contract with no recovery mechanism.

findings.title: LP Tokens Burned via safeTransfer to address(0)
findings.description: LP tokens are burned by transferring to address(0). This works for UniswapV2 which allows transfers to address(0), but relies on non-standard behavior. Standard ERC20 implementations would revert on transfer to address(0), creating a deployment risk on other chains or with different LP token implementations.

findings.title: Direct vETH Transfer to Pool Can Manipulate Reserves
findings.description: Whitelisted entities can transfer vETH directly to pools, bypassing AMM price discovery mechanisms. This allows manipulation of pool reserves outside of normal swap operations. Requires a trusted whitelisted entity to execute, so risk is limited under the current trust model.

findings.title: Rebalance cashOut Path Solvency Concern
findings.description: The complex flow of vETH between V2, V3, and rebalance contract creates theoretical solvency questions when vETH is moved between pools. Analysis confirms the debt lock mechanism maintains the invariant (transferable_balance = balance - debt) under normal conditions, but edge cases in the rebalance flow warrant monitoring.

findings.title: UniswapV2Library.pairFor() Hardcoded Init Code Hash
findings.description: Hardcoded Uniswap V2 init code hash is correct for Ethereum mainnet but creates a deployment landmine for any other chain. If deployed on a chain with a different Uniswap V2 factory or modified init code, pairFor() would compute wrong addresses, silently sending funds to non-existent pools.

findings.title: Rebalancer extractProfit() Cannot Extract Native ETH
findings.description: The extractProfit() function only handles ERC20 tokens. Any native ETH that accumulates in the rebalance contract (from WETH unwrapping edge cases or direct transfers) is permanently irrecoverable with no fallback extraction mechanism.

findings.title: Router Has No Asset Extraction Function
findings.description: The router accumulates 1 wei per buy transaction (off-by-one refund) and may receive accidental ETH or ERC20 transfers, but has no extraction function for ETH or ERC20 tokens. All accumulated assets are permanently locked in the contract.
